Question:
A \(\bigtriangleup\) or \(\bigcirc\) is placed in each of the nine squares in a \(3 \times 3\) grid. Shown below is a sample configuration with three \(\bigtriangleup\)’s in a line.

[Figure 1](figures/2022_AMC_8_Q23_question_fig1.svg)

How many configurations will have three \(\bigtriangleup\)’s in a line and three \(\bigcirc\)’s in a line?
Solution:
A triangle line and a circle line cannot share a square. Any diagonal intersects every possible three-square line, and every row intersects every column. Thus the two lines must be in different rows or in different columns.

First count arrangements using rows. If exactly one row is all triangles and exactly one is all circles, there are \(3\cdot2=6\) ways to choose those rows. The remaining row has \(2^3=8\) possible patterns, but the two uniform patterns would create a second uniform row. Excluding those leaves \(6\) choices, giving \(6\cdot6=36\) arrangements.

The remaining case has two uniform rows of one symbol and one uniform row of the other. Choose the majority symbol in \(2\) ways and the minority row in \(3\) ways, giving \(6\) arrangements.

There are therefore \(36+6=42\) row arrangements. The same count applies to columns. These cases cannot overlap: an all-triangle row prevents an all-circle column, and conversely.

The total is \(2\cdot42=\boxed{84}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\). Separating the all-uniform case prevents an arrangement from being counted twice.
